author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Price of Welcome
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The pantry shelves looked fuller from the doorway.

It was an optical illusion caused by the jars in the front row. Behind them, the flour sack was nearly empty, the last dried beans had been marked for the clinic, and the vegetable crates contained more leaves than vegetables.

Mara stood with the inventory sheet in her hand.

"Don't say it's fine," she warned.

"I wasn't going to."

"Everyone does."

I stepped beside her and looked at the figures.

A flood upstream had blocked the lower cart route for several days. Deliveries were using the longer ridge path. The pantry had fed the repair crews, provided emergency meals for two visiting families, and supplied the clinic volunteers without charging people who had arrived with nothing.

Nobody had done anything wrong by needing food.

But the jars didn't refill because we had been kind.

Maui appeared carrying his hook.

"I'll fish."

Mara looked at him.

"How many?"

"As many as we need."

"Who cleans them? Who salts them? Who stores them? Who makes sure the people who can't eat fish have something else?"

Maui blinked.

"Fish is food."

"Not the only food."

I heard Katara's voice behind us.

"And a fresh catch won't survive a week in warm weather without proper handling."

She had come to check the clinic supplies and brought two volunteers with her. One of them had written down the meals people could actually eat, including allergies and religious or personal restrictions they had chosen to disclose.

Katara put the sheet on the table.

"Let's start with what the families need. Then we can decide which supplies will help."

Maui looked disappointed.

"Fishing still helps."

"Of course it does," Katara said. "If the work after catching the fish is planned."

That was fair. It was also not a thrilling beginning to an emergency.

We called a pantry meeting.

Mara brought the ledger. Fen brought the tide chart and information about the safest fishing hours. Tamsin described which carts could use the ridge. Iroh offered an inexpensive soup recipe that used less fuel than several smaller meals. Greg volunteered to help distribute food but asked to be given a definite shift rather than a promise to appear whenever needed.

Edda spoke about delivery access. Some families could reach the square, others couldn't. A meal on a high shelf wasn't useful to a person who couldn't lift it down.

I made a list of offers.

Then I caught myself assigning names to jobs.

"Wait," I said.

Everyone looked up.

"I've written Greg on the evening delivery without asking whether he's free."

Greg raised a hand.

"I'm not. I said tomorrow morning."

I crossed out the shift.

"Sorry."

Mara grinned.

"Congratulations. You caught yourself before we had to."

The meeting took an hour. We planned three days of meals, set aside the clinic's medically necessary supplies, and wrote a public notice explaining which items were short without listing which families had requested help.

Maui agreed to fish with Fen during the safe tide window. Two people who knew food handling volunteered to prepare the catch, and Mara allocated salt from the bakery stores with a clear repayment plan. The pantry would buy vegetables from the next available cart rather than assume someone would donate them.

None of the numbers were comfortable.

They were workable.

The next morning I went with Maui to the landing.

He was quiet while Fen checked the lines. The sea was calm, but the water carried branches and silt from the upstream flood. We used the upper route and kept the boat close to shore.

Maui caught three fish.

Then he stopped.

I looked at him.

"Only three?"

"Fen says the small ones need to stay."

Fen nodded.

"Breeding season. Take the adults, leave the young, and we might still have fish next month."

Maui looked at the water.

"I used to think feeding people meant bringing home the biggest possible catch."

"And now?"

"Now it means making sure the sea can feed them again."

I smiled.

We took the fish to the cleaning station, where Mara's cousin was waiting. Maui offered to help with the work. She handed him an apron.

He stared at it.

"You want me to wear that?"

"Unless you enjoy smelling like fish for three days."

He put it on.

By afternoon the first meals were ready. The clinic received its share. The two visiting families chose from the available options, without having to explain publicly why they needed help. Edda checked that the delivery station was accessible from the level path.

Iroh asked Mara whether she wanted more soup tomorrow. She studied the pantry list before answering.

"Not unless you can bring clean jars back," she said. "We don't have enough containers for another large delivery."

"Then I shall bring the soup in what I have and collect the empties after."

Mara nodded. I watched how the exchange left both people free to decide what they could actually provide. There was no miracle pot that filled itself, and Iroh didn't pretend his tea shop could feed a valley forever.

A child arrived with a note from the clinic, asking whether the next delivery could include something easier to carry up the hill. Edda checked the route before we agreed to a new time. Maui looked at the note and then toward the sea.

"I could deliver it in one trip," he said.

"Probably," I answered. "But can the next volunteer do the same?"

He made a face. "You're ruining all the fun."

"Just the kind that requires you to be here every time."

We divided the delivery into smaller loads that ordinary people could carry. Mara recorded the change; a new worker would be able to follow it without having to guess what we'd intended.

When we finished, the apron around Maui's waist was damp and smelled terrible. I couldn't stop smiling at him.

"What?" he demanded.

"Nothing. You're a fearsome fisher."

"I am a legend."

"With fish scales in your hair."

He tried to brush them away and made it worse. I laughed so hard I had to hold the edge of the table.

His eyes softened. "I like making you laugh."

"I like laughing."

"Can I kiss you before the work starts again?"

I nodded, and he leaned close enough that I could smell salt and clean soap beneath the fish. The kiss was brief, gentle, and decidedly less heroic than anything he'd planned for the morning.

Then Mara called us back to the loading list. The pantry remained short on flour, but its deliveries had a plan that didn't require our presence at every meal. It felt like a better kind of generosity.

Iroh brought a pot of soup.

Toph tasted it and declared it "suspiciously sensible."

Katara laughed.

The pantry wasn't saved forever. A storm could block the ridge again. A harvest could fail. Someone could need more help than we'd planned.

That was why we wrote down what worked and what didn't.

After dinner, Mara counted the remaining stock.

"We have enough for the next three days," she said.

"Just three?"

"Three is real. A week would be a promise we haven't earned."

I looked at the figures.

For once, I didn't try to make them prettier.

Maui found me at the table after the others left.

"You're worried."

"Yes."

"About the pantry?"

"About how often welcome means somebody quietly doing more than they can afford."

He sat beside me.

"I thought I could solve it by fishing all night."

"I know."

"I like doing something big."

"You also wore an apron today."

He groaned.

"Do not tell anyone."

"I have already told three people."

"Jasper."

I laughed and leaned against him.

He turned his face toward mine.

"Would you like me to stay with you tonight?" he asked.

"Yes."

"Quietly?"

"Mostly."

He smiled.

He kissed me softly, then kissed me again when I caught his sleeve. There was flour on my hands and a smear of salt on his wrist. I had never found a pantry inventory particularly romantic before.

But there was something tender about a person willing to do the ordinary part of caring.

The next morning we went back to the square to help unload the ridge cart. It was late, muddy, and carrying fewer vegetables than we'd hoped.

Mara looked at the crates and sighed.

Then she opened the ledger.

We began again.
